title: Diction and Syntax
bigQuestion: If two writers describe the same room with the same facts, why does one paragraph feel calm and the other feel like a storm?

story.title: Two Paragraphs, One Room
story.kicker: A teacher hands out two descriptions of the same hospital waiting room, written by two students, and asks the class which one is nervous.
paragraphs: Ms. Okafor put two paragraphs on the board without names. Both described the same thing: a hospital waiting room at two in the morning, a boy waiting to hear about his father. The facts were identical. Same room, same boy, same clock on the wall, same vending machine humming in the corner. She asked the class one question: which writer is more afraid? Nobody could point to a single word that said afraid. Yet within thirty seconds, every hand pointed to the first paragraph.

The first paragraph was built the way Ernest Hemingway built his: short, plain sentences, most of them under ten words. The boy sat. The clock said two. A door opened and it was not the doctor. The words were small and common, the kind you learn by second grade. No sentence explained how the boy felt. The reader had to sit in the gaps between the sentences, and the gaps were where the fear lived. The paragraph did not run; it held its breath.

The second paragraph was built the way William Faulkner built his: one sentence that went on for six lines, clause piled on clause, the room and the boy's memories and the smell of the floor cleaner and the sound of his mother's voice on the phone an hour earlier all braided together without a period in sight. The words were bigger and more unusual. The sentence did not hold its breath; it could not stop talking. It was afraid too, but its fear was a flood instead of a held breath.

That is the whole point of this chapter. The first paragraph did not say 'short sentences feel tense.' The second did not say 'long sentences feel overwhelmed.' They just were those things, and every reader in the room felt it before anyone could name it. A writer's *style* is not decoration added at the end. It is the sum of the choices about which words and which sentence shapes to use, and those choices carry meaning as surely as the facts do.

By the end of the chapter you will be able to look at any paragraph and say precisely what it is doing: what level its words are pitched at, how its sentences are shaped, where it puts its weight, and how fast it moves. You will also be able to do it on purpose in your own writing, which is the difference between having a style and having one happen to you.
story.think: The class felt the difference before anyone could explain it. What would you have to look at in each paragraph to move from 'I feel it' to 'here is exactly why'?

lessons.title: Levels of Diction
lessons.mainIdea: Diction is word choice, and every word sits at a level, from formal to casual, that tells the reader how to take the sentence.
reading: Read these three sentences, all about the same event. 'The gentleman departed from the residence.' 'The man left the house.' 'The guy took off.' Nothing about the facts changed. A male person went away from a building. What changed is the *diction*, the writer's choice of words. Each version sits at a different level, and each level tells the reader something about who is speaking, to whom, and how seriously.

Writers usually talk about three levels. *Formal* diction uses longer, often Latin-based words, no contractions and no slang: 'departed,' 'residence,' 'commence.' It sounds like a legal document, a scholarly article or a ceremony. *Standard* (sometimes called middle) diction uses ordinary, correct English that most readers use every day: 'left,' 'house,' 'begin.' Most published writing lives here. *Informal* or *colloquial* diction is the language of talk: 'took off,' 'guy,' 'kick things off.' It includes slang and contractions and sounds like a person, not a page.

No level is better than the others. The question is fit. A eulogy in slang would feel disrespectful; a text to a friend in formal diction would feel like a joke. Skilled writers move between levels on purpose, and the move itself carries meaning. When a formal paragraph suddenly drops to 'and then it all fell apart,' the drop lands hard because the reader feels the level change. When you analyze a passage, name the level first. Then ask why the writer chose it, and look for the moments where it shifts.

words.d: a writer's choice of words, including how formal or casual they are
elevated word choice with no slang or contractions, often using longer Latin-based words
the informal language of everyday speech, including slang and contractions
where a word sits on the scale from formal to casual

look.title: Formal Word, Plain Word
look.prompt: The formal word in each pair has more syllables than its plain twin. What does that pattern suggest about why formal diction feels slower and heavier to read?

check.q: What is diction?
choices: The order of words in a sentence
The main idea of a text
check.why: Diction is word choice; the order of words is syntax, which comes later in the chapter.

check.q: 'The guy took off' is an example of which level of diction?
check.why: 'Guy' and 'took off' are the language of casual talk, which is colloquial or informal diction.

check.q: Why does the lesson say no level of diction is better than the others?
choices: Because readers cannot tell the levels apart
Because formal diction is always correct
Because the right level depends on the audience and occasion
Because all published writing uses the same level
check.why: Fit is the test: a eulogy in slang or a text to a friend in formal words both fail because the level does not match the situation.

lessons.title: Connotation Inside a Sentence
lessons.mainIdea: A word's connotation is the feeling it carries beyond its definition, and one swapped word can turn a whole sentence toward praise or blame.
reading: 'The senator was thrifty.' 'The senator was cheap.' 'The senator was stingy.' Look up all three words and you will find nearly the same *denotation*, the dictionary meaning: careful with money. Yet the first sentence is a compliment, the second a shrug, and the third an insult. The difference is *connotation*, the cloud of feeling and association that travels with a word. Thrifty carries pictures of a wise grandmother. Stingy carries a picture of a closed fist.

You learned connotation as a word-level idea years ago. At this level you need to see how it works across a whole sentence, where several connotations add up. 'The crowd surged toward the stage' and 'The mob swarmed toward the stage' describe the same people moving the same way. But crowd is neutral and mob is dangerous; surged is energetic and swarmed is insect-like. Stack two loaded words and the sentence now takes a side without ever stating an opinion. That is why connotation matters so much in news writing, in political speech and in your own essays.

When you analyze a passage, do not just say 'the writer uses connotation.' Everyone does. Instead, find the loaded words, name the direction they lean, and explain what the sentence would lose if a neutral word replaced them. Try it on this line written for the lesson: 'The old house squatted at the end of the lane.' Replace squatted with stood. The house is the same shape, but stood is upright and calm, while squatted is low, heavy and a little ugly. The writer chose squatted so you would dislike the house before anyone walks in.

words.d: the literal, dictionary definition of a word
the feelings and associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning
a word chosen for its strong positive or negative connotation
carrying no strong feeling for or against

look.title: One Verb, Three Readers
look.text: A reporter writes three drafts of the same fact. Draft one: 'The mayor admitted the budget was late.' Draft two: 'The mayor announced the budget was late.' Draft three: 'The mayor confessed the budget was late.' The mayor said the same words in every draft.
look.prompt: Which draft makes the mayor look guilty, which makes her look in control, and which verb would a careful editor call the most neutral? Explain how you know.

check.q: What is the difference between denotation and connotation?
choices: Denotation is the spelling; connotation is the pronunciation
Denotation is the formal use; connotation is the slang use
Denotation applies to nouns; connotation applies to verbs
Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling a word carries
check.why: Thrifty, cheap and stingy share a denotation (careful with money) but carry very different feelings, which is their connotation.

check.q: In 'The mob swarmed toward the stage,' what do the words mob and swarmed do together?
choices: They make the sentence take a side without stating an opinion
They make the sentence more formal
They describe a different event than 'the crowd surged'
check.why: Both words are loaded with danger, so the sentence judges the people while pretending only to describe them.

check.q: Why does the lesson say replacing squatted with stood changes the house?
choices: Because stood is a longer word
Because squatted makes the house feel low and unpleasant while stood is calm
Because squatted is a grammar error
Because stood changes the shape of the house
check.why: The house is physically the same; only the reader's feeling about it changes, which is what connotation does.

lessons.title: Register and Audience
lessons.mainIdea: Register is the level of language you choose for a particular audience and situation, and matching it is the first job of any writer.
reading: A student writes to her principal: 'hey can u move my exam, thx.' Nothing is misspelled on purpose, and the request is clear. It still fails, because it is pitched in the wrong *register*. Register is the version of the language you select for a specific audience, purpose and situation. You already own several registers. You do not talk to a toddler, a coach, a judge and your best friend in the same way, and you did not have to be taught that. Writing asks you to make the same choice on paper, where you cannot see the listener's face.

Register combines the diction levels from the first lesson with other choices: contractions or none, first person or not, sentence length, how much you explain, whether you joke. A lab report is in a high, impersonal register: 'The solution was heated to 80 degrees.' A group chat is in a low, personal one: 'ok we're heating it, this is taking forever.' A college application essay lives in between: personal and warm but grammatically careful, with no slang. The most common failure in student writing is not bad grammar. It is a register mismatch, sounding like a text message in an essay or like a lawyer in a story.

To choose a register, ask three questions before you write. Who will read this, and what do they expect? What do I want them to do or feel? What would sound wrong here? Then hold the register steady, because a slip is loud. A cover letter that says 'I am highly motivated and, like, super organized' loses the reader at 'like.' When you read a professional writer, notice how consistent the register is, and notice the rare moments when it breaks on purpose to make you laugh or flinch.

words.d: the variety of language a speaker or writer selects to fit a particular audience and situation
the people who will read or hear a piece of writing
a register that does not fit its audience or purpose

look.title: Four Readers, One Message
look.text: You broke your wrist and cannot type for two weeks. You need to tell four people: your best friend, your English teacher, your manager at the grocery store, and the scholarship office that is waiting on your essay. The facts are identical in every message.
look.prompt: Draft the first sentence of each message. What changed between them, and which one was hardest to get right?

check.q: What is register?
choices: A list of a writer's favorite words
The rhythm of sentences in a paragraph
The variety of language chosen to fit an audience and situation
The correct spelling of formal words
check.why: Register is the version of the language you pick for the people you are addressing and the reason you are addressing them.

check.q: According to the lesson, what is the most common failure in student writing?
check.why: The lesson says students most often fail by sounding like a text in an essay or a lawyer in a story, not by breaking grammar rules.

check.q: Why does 'like, super organized' hurt a cover letter?
choices: Because organization is not a skill employers want
Because cover letters must not use adjectives
Because the casual words break the professional register the letter had set
check.why: A register slip is loud; the reader hears the wrong voice and stops trusting the writer.

sections.title: Syntax: The Shape of the Sentence

lessons.title: Sentence Length and Pace
lessons.mainIdea: Syntax is sentence structure, and the simplest syntax choice, how long each sentence runs, sets the pace a reader feels.
reading: Passage A, written for this lesson: 'The door was open. Nobody was home. She set the bag down and waited.' Passage B: 'Because the door stood open onto an empty house that still smelled of the morning's coffee, she set the bag on the counter and waited for a sound that did not come.' Same door, same bag, same waiting. Passage A is three sentences totaling fourteen words. Passage B is one sentence of thirty-two. Read them aloud and you will feel the difference in your chest. A is tense and clipped. B is slow and full.

*Syntax* is the arrangement of words into phrases, clauses and sentences. Length is its most visible feature. Short sentences make the reader stop often, and each stop is a small beat of silence, so a string of short sentences feels urgent, blunt or stunned. Long sentences carry the reader across many ideas without a stop, so they feel thoughtful, flowing or, if they go on too long, exhausting. Neither is right in itself. A writer controls *pace*, the speed at which a reader moves, largely by varying length.

The strongest effect comes from contrast. A long sentence followed by a short one makes the short one hit like a door slamming. Read this: 'She had rehearsed the speech for a week, timed it, cut it, practiced it in the mirror and in the shower and on the bus, until every pause was planned. Then the microphone died.' The second sentence is only four words, and it lands because the first was thirty. When you analyze a passage, count. Actual numbers, average length and the range from shortest to longest, make your claim about pace something a reader can check.

words.d: the arrangement of words into phrases, clauses and sentences
the speed at which a reader moves through a text, controlled largely by sentence length
short and abrupt, as in a series of very brief sentences

look.title: Words per Sentence, Two Passages
look.prompt: Passage B has one sentence that is longer than all of Passage A put together. Where would a reader of B first get to breathe, and how does that change the feeling of waiting?

check.q: What is syntax?
choices: The arrangement of words into phrases, clauses and sentences
The choice of formal or informal words
check.why: Syntax is sentence structure; diction is word choice.

check.q: What effect does a string of short sentences usually create?
choices: A sense of urgency or bluntness
check.why: Each period is a stop, and many stops in a row make the reader feel tension or shock.

check.q: Why does 'Then the microphone died' hit so hard?
choices: Because it uses a loaded word
Because it is in the passive voice
Because it is very short after a very long sentence
check.why: Contrast is the key: the four-word sentence lands like a slammed door after a thirty-word sentence.

lessons.title: Word Order and Inversion
lessons.mainIdea: English expects subject, then verb, then object; when a writer inverts that order, the moved word grabs attention.
reading: English is a word-order language. 'The dog bit the man' and 'The man bit the dog' use the same four words and mean opposite things, because the subject normally comes first, then the verb, then the object. Readers expect that order so strongly that when a sentence breaks it, they notice, even if they cannot say what they noticed. *Inversion* is the deliberate reversal of the usual order, and writers use it to throw weight onto a word that would otherwise sit unnoticed.

Compare: 'The letter came at last' and 'At last the letter came.' In the second, the writer has pulled 'at last' to the front, and the relief in those two words now opens the sentence. Compare 'I have never seen such a mess' with 'Never have I seen such a mess.' The inverted version sounds older, more emphatic, almost theatrical, because the negative word leads and forces the verb ahead of the subject. Poets and orators love this move. Lincoln's Gettysburg Address begins 'Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth,' putting the time first, so the sentence opens like a door into history instead of starting flatly with 'Our fathers.'

Inversion is a spice, not a meal. One inverted sentence in a paragraph draws the eye; five in a row sound like a wizard in a movie. The other everyday form of reordering is simpler: moving a phrase to the front or the end. 'She signed the contract, reluctantly' and 'Reluctantly, she signed the contract' put the same word in the two positions readers remember most, the very end and the very beginning. When you analyze syntax, look for anything that is not in its expected place. Then ask what the writer gained by moving it.

words.d: reversing the normal subject-verb-object order of a sentence for emphasis
the sequence of subject, verb and object that English readers expect
extra weight or attention placed on a particular word or idea

look.title: Lincoln Opens with Time
look.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
look.prompt: Rewrite the sentence so it begins with 'Our fathers.' What is lost when the time phrase is moved off the front, and why do you think Lincoln wanted it there?

check.q: What is the normal word order of an English sentence?
check.why: 'The dog bit the man' shows the expected order: subject (dog), verb (bit), object (man).

check.q: What does inversion do to the word that is moved?
choices: Makes it stand out to the reader
check.why: Because readers expect the usual order, a word pulled out of place draws attention.

check.q: Why does the lesson call inversion 'a spice, not a meal'?
choices: Because it only works in poetry
Because it is used too often in cooking shows
Because a little draws the eye but too much sounds strange
Because it is a grammar error
check.why: One inverted sentence is striking; a whole paragraph of them sounds artificial.

lessons.title: Periodic and Loose Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: A loose sentence gives its main point first and adds on; a periodic sentence holds the main point until the end, building suspense.
reading: Two sentences, written for this lesson. First: 'She passed the exam, after three months of studying every night, two failed practice tests and a week of barely sleeping.' Second: 'After three months of studying every night, two failed practice tests and a week of barely sleeping, she passed the exam.' The words are the same. The first one tells you the outcome in four words and then trails the details behind it. The second makes you wait through all the details before you learn what happened.

The first is a *loose sentence* (also called cumulative): the main clause comes early, and phrases and clauses accumulate after it. You could stop it at almost any comma and still have a complete thought. Loose sentences feel natural, relaxed and conversational, because that is how people talk. The second is a *periodic sentence*: the main clause is delayed until the end, so the sentence is not grammatically complete until its last words. Periodic sentences build suspense and land with force, because the reader has been holding all those details, waiting for the point.

Lincoln's opening sentence at Gettysburg is loose: 'our fathers brought forth' comes early, and the modifiers pile up after it. Many famous last lines are periodic, since the delay makes the ending ring. Neither shape is better. A paragraph of only periodic sentences would exhaust a reader, who would always be waiting; a paragraph of only loose ones can feel slack. When you analyze a passage, spot where the main clause sits. Early means loose, late means periodic, and a shift from one to the other usually marks a moment the writer wants you to feel.

words.d: a sentence whose main clause comes first, with details added after; also called cumulative
a sentence that delays its main clause until the end, creating suspense
the part of a sentence that could stand alone as a complete thought
the tension of waiting to learn what will happen or what the point is

look.title: Douglass Turns a Sentence Around
look.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
look.cite: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
look.prompt: The two halves mirror each other with the words reversed. Where does the sentence put its weight, and how would it change if Douglass had written the second half first?

check.q: In a periodic sentence, where does the main clause appear?
check.why: A periodic sentence delays the main clause until the end, so the reader waits for the point.

check.q: Why do loose sentences feel conversational?
choices: Because they give the point first and add details the way people talk
check.why: People naturally state a thing and then tack on details; loose sentences mirror that habit.

check.q: What would likely happen if a writer used only periodic sentences for a whole page?
choices: The reader would grow tired of always waiting for the point
The writing would feel too casual
check.why: Suspense works by contrast; constant delay wears the reader out.

lessons.title: Fragments on Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: A sentence fragment is an error when it is an accident and a tool when it is a choice, and skilled writers use fragments for emphasis.
reading: You have been told for years that a sentence fragment is wrong. In a lab report or a college application, it still is. But open almost any novel or magazine essay and you will find fragments doing deliberate work. Written for this lesson: 'He checked the lock twice, then the windows, then the lock again. Nothing. Just the wind.' 'Nothing' has no verb and no subject. 'Just the wind' has no verb. Both are *fragments*, and both are exactly right, because they sound like the man's mind, checking and finding.

A fragment works when it is clearly a choice. Three signs tell the reader it is on purpose. It is short. It sits after a complete sentence that sets it up. And it carries a single strong beat: an answer, a correction, a punch. 'She said she would call. She didn't. Not once.' The fragment 'Not once' hammers the point that the complete sentence already made. A fragment fails when it is long, wandering and unattached, like 'Which is the reason that I decided, after talking with my counselor about my options for the fall semester.' That is not a beat. That is a sentence that lost its main clause on the way.

Two cautions. First, know your audience: fragments belong in narrative, personal essays, speeches and ads, not in formal academic or professional writing, where readers will assume you made a mistake. Second, ration them. One fragment in a paragraph is a drumbeat. Six is a drum solo, and readers stop hearing the beat. When you analyze a passage and find fragments, do not mark them as errors. Ask what each one emphasizes and why the writer chose a broken sentence over a whole one at that exact spot.

words.d: a group of words punctuated as a sentence but lacking a subject, a verb or a complete thought
done on purpose, as a choice
a single strong moment of emphasis, like one strike of a drum

look.title: Poe's Narrator Breaks His Sentences
look.text: True! --nervous --very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
look.prompt: The opening word 'True!' stands alone, and the dashes chop the next phrase into pieces. What do these broken units tell you about the narrator before he says a single fact?

check.q: When is a sentence fragment a tool rather than an error?
choices: When it is longer than the sentence before it
When it appears in a lab report
When it is a short, clear choice that adds emphasis
When it contains a subject and a verb
check.why: The lesson's three signs are that it is short, set up by a complete sentence, and carries one strong beat.

check.q: In 'She said she would call. She didn't. Not once.' what does the fragment do?
choices: It makes the paragraph more formal
It hammers the point the previous sentence made
check.why: 'Not once' repeats and sharpens the emphasis of 'She didn't.'

check.q: Where does the lesson say fragments do NOT belong?
check.why: In formal writing, readers assume a fragment is a mistake, so the emphasis is lost.

lessons.title: Where the Weight Falls
lessons.mainIdea: Readers remember the end of a sentence most and the beginning next, so a writer controls emphasis by what goes in those two slots.
reading: Read these two sentences. 'The bridge collapsed at 4:15 on a Tuesday afternoon.' 'At 4:15 on a Tuesday afternoon, the bridge collapsed.' Both are grammatical and both are clear. But in the first, the last thing in your ear is the day of the week. In the second, the last thing in your ear is the collapse. The second sentence is about a disaster; the first sounds almost like a schedule. The facts are identical. The *emphasis* moved because the words at the end moved.

Writers call this *end focus* (some say end weight): the final position in a sentence is the position of greatest stress, and the opening position is second. The middle is where things go to be forgotten. This gives you a rule you can actually use. Put the word you most want remembered at the end of the sentence. Put the idea that connects to the previous sentence at the beginning. Bury the routine details, dates, minor names, qualifications, in the middle. 'The report, which ran to two hundred pages and took eleven months, recommended closing the plant' sends the reader out on 'closing the plant,' which is the news.

Punctuation shapes emphasis too. A colon points forward like a finger: whatever follows it is announced. A dash sets a phrase apart so it stands alone for a second. Parentheses whisper; whatever is inside them is marked as less important. Repetition builds weight the way a hammer does, one strike after another, which is why speeches repeat their key phrases. When you analyze a passage for emphasis, find the last word of each sentence and read those last words in a column. In good prose, that column is a summary of what the writer wanted you to keep.

words.d: the tendency of readers to give the most weight to the final words of a sentence
the extra attention a position in a sentence receives
a detail that limits or narrows a claim, such as a date or a condition

look.title: Lincoln's Last Words at Gettysburg
look.text: that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address, 1863 (the closing words)
look.prompt: The speech ends on 'the earth.' Rewrite the clause so it ends on 'the people' instead. Which ending feels larger, and what does the triple repetition of 'the people' do before the final word arrives?

check.q: Which position in a sentence carries the most emphasis for readers?
check.why: End focus means the final words get the heaviest stress; the opening is second, and the middle is where details are buried.

check.q: Why does 'At 4:15 on a Tuesday afternoon, the bridge collapsed' feel more like a disaster than the other version?
choices: Because it uses more formal words
Because the collapse now sits at the end where it gets the most weight
Because the time is no longer mentioned
check.why: Moving 'the bridge collapsed' to the end puts the event in the stressed position.

check.q: According to the lesson, what do parentheses signal about the words inside them?
choices: That they are the main point
That they should be read aloud louder
check.why: Parentheses whisper; they mark the enclosed words as a side note.

lessons.title: Analyzing a Passage Precisely
lessons.mainIdea: A precise style analysis names specific choices in diction and syntax, shows them in the text, and explains the effect each one creates.
reading: Weak style analysis sounds like this: 'The author uses diction and syntax to create a mood.' Every author does. That sentence could be stapled to any passage ever written, which means it says nothing. Strong analysis sounds like this: 'The passage relies on one- and two-syllable words and sentences averaging seven words, and the only long sentence, twenty-six words, arrives at the moment the narrator finally sees the letter, so the syntax slows exactly where the narrator's attention does.' The second version names a choice, measures it and ties it to a place in the text and an effect.

Use a routine. First, read the passage twice, once for meaning and once for sound, ideally aloud. Second, mark the diction: circle words that are unusually formal, unusually plain, loaded, technical or repeated. Third, mark the syntax: note sentence lengths, any fragments, any inversion, where main clauses sit, what each sentence ends on. Fourth, look for the shift, because almost every good passage changes somewhere, from long to short, from formal to blunt, from loose to periodic. Fifth, connect each choice to an effect and, above all, to the passage's purpose. The question is never just 'what does the writer do' but 'what does it do to the reader, and why would the writer want that?'

Write the analysis in the pattern of claim, evidence, effect. Claim: the writer's sentences shorten as the danger grows. Evidence: the first paragraph averages nineteen words per sentence; the last averages six, ending in a two-word fragment. Effect: the reader's breath shortens with the sentences, so the fear is felt rather than announced. Use the technical terms from this chapter, but only where they earn their place. 'Periodic' is useful when it explains why an ending lands. It is noise when it is just a word you learned.

words.d: an explanation of how a writer's specific choices in words and sentences create effects
the point in a passage where the style changes, often marking a turn in meaning
what a choice does to the reader: a feeling, a pace, an emphasis
what the writer wants the passage to accomplish

look.title: Two Sentences of Analysis
look.text: Student A writes: 'Poe uses short sentences and scary words to make the reader feel nervous.' Student B writes: 'Poe's narrator opens with a one-word exclamation and then breaks his second sentence with three dashes, so that the syntax stutters like a man protesting too much, before he ever mentions the old man or the eye.'
look.prompt: Both students noticed real things. What does Student B do that Student A does not, and which of the five steps of the routine did Student A skip?

check.q: Why is 'The author uses diction and syntax to create a mood' a weak sentence of analysis?
choices: Because it could describe any passage and names no specific choice
Because mood is not part of style
check.why: Analysis must name a particular choice, show it in the text and explain its effect; a sentence true of every text does none of that.

check.q: What does the lesson say almost every good passage contains?
check.why: Step four of the routine is to find the shift, from long to short, formal to blunt, and so on.

check.q: In the claim-evidence-effect pattern, what is the evidence for a claim about pace?
choices: Actual sentence lengths from the passage
The reader's opinion of the story
The definition of the word pace
check.why: Counts such as average words per sentence make the claim checkable.

lessons.title: Imitating a Style
lessons.mainIdea: Imitation, writing your own content in another writer's sentence shapes, is the fastest way to feel a style from the inside.
reading: Musicians learn by playing other people's songs. Painters copy the masters in museums. Writers, for centuries, have done the same thing: taken a sentence they admire and written a new one in its exact shape, with their own subject. This is *imitation*, and it is not cheating, because you keep the structure and change every word. It teaches you what analysis alone cannot, which is how a sentence feels to build.

Here is the method. Take a model sentence. Written for this lesson: 'After the storm, when the streets were still black with water and the power had not come back, the neighbors carried out chairs and sat in the dark together.' Map it: introductory phrase, then a 'when' clause with two parts joined by 'and,' then the main clause with a compound verb and a final phrase. Now write your own sentence in the same slots. 'Before the exam, when the hallway was still loud with rumors and the doors had not opened, the students spread out notes and quizzed each other on the floor.' Same architecture, new building.

Do this with sentences of different shapes: a periodic sentence, a loose one, a three-word sentence after a long one, a passage with a fragment. Then do it with a whole paragraph, keeping the pattern of lengths. You will notice things you never saw as a reader: how hard it is to hold a periodic sentence together, how a fragment needs a strong sentence in front of it. Afterward, the shapes are yours. You will find them showing up in your own drafts, in your own voice, which is exactly how every writer you admire learned to write.

words.d: writing new content in the exact sentence structure of a model, as a way to learn a style
a sentence or passage used as a pattern to copy the structure of
the underlying arrangement of a sentence's parts

look.title: Dickens Builds a Sentence of Pairs
look.text: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness,
look.cite: Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, 1859 (the opening words)
look.prompt: Map the pattern: 'it was the ___ of ___' repeated with opposites. Write four clauses in the same shape about your school, your city or this year. What does the pattern force you to think about?

check.q: In imitation, what do you keep and what do you change?
choices: Keep the words, change the order
Keep the structure, change the words
Keep the topic, change the length
Keep the first sentence, change the rest
check.why: Imitation preserves the sentence's architecture while replacing all of its content.

check.q: Why does the lesson say imitation is not cheating?
choices: Because the model is public domain
Because you keep only the structure and write every word yourself
Because you cite the original author
check.why: The content is entirely yours; only the shape is borrowed, and shapes cannot be owned.

check.q: What does imitation teach that analysis alone cannot?
choices: How a sentence feels to build from the inside
check.why: Building a periodic sentence yourself shows you why it is hard and what it costs, which reading about it does not.

lessons.title: Voice as a Set of Choices
lessons.mainIdea: A writer's voice is not a mystery gift; it is the pattern of diction and syntax choices the writer makes over and over.
reading: People talk about a writer's *voice* as if it were something you are born with, like the sound of your speaking voice. It is not. Voice on the page is a pattern: the level of diction a writer returns to, the sentence lengths they favor, how often they use fragments, whether they like periodic suspense or loose ease, what they put at the ends of sentences, whether they joke. Read enough of one writer and you can recognize a paragraph without a name on it, the way you recognize a friend's walk from across a parking lot. What you are recognizing is the sum of the choices.

This is good news, because it means voice can be worked on. Walt Whitman's voice comes from long, listing lines, plain and physical nouns, and a first person that keeps addressing the reader directly: 'I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume.' Emily Dickinson's voice comes from short lines, dashes that interrupt, unexpected capital letters and abstract nouns treated like people: 'Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –.' Neither poet was mysterious. Each made a small set of choices with great consistency.

To find your own voice, stop looking for it and start choosing. Take a paragraph you wrote and ask the chapter's questions of it. What level is your diction, and does it shift on purpose? How long are your sentences, and do they vary? Where does your weight fall? Then decide what you want more of. A writer who chooses short declaratives and plain nouns for a year will have a voice, and it will be theirs. Style is not the clothes a piece of writing wears. It is the way it moves, and you decide how it moves.

words.d: the recognizable pattern of a writer's choices in diction, syntax and tone
a plain statement sentence, as opposed to a question, command or exclamation
making the same kinds of choices again and again

look.title: Two Poets Describe the Same Rain
look.text: Imagine the same summer rain written by two poets. One writes long lines that list every roof, gutter, bus and face the rain touches, and keeps saying 'you' to the reader. The other writes four-word lines cut by dashes, and calls the rain 'a Visitor' with a capital V.
look.prompt: Which description sounds like Whitman and which like Dickinson? Name at least three specific choices, not feelings, that let you tell them apart.

check.q: According to the lesson, what is a writer's voice?
choices: The sound of the writer reading aloud
A talent some writers are born with
The pattern of choices a writer makes in diction and syntax
check.why: Voice is the sum of repeated choices, which is why it can be recognized and worked on.

check.q: Which set of choices does the lesson attribute to Dickinson?
choices: Long listing lines and direct address to the reader
Short lines, dashes and unexpected capitals
Formal Latin-based diction and periodic sentences
check.why: The lesson names short lines, interrupting dashes and capitalized abstract nouns as Dickinson's pattern.

check.q: What does the lesson advise a student who wants to find a voice?
choices: Stop searching and start making consistent choices
check.why: Voice is built by choosing, so the advice is to choose deliberately and consistently.

review.q: 'The gentleman departed from the residence' is written in which level of diction?
review.why: Departed and residence are longer Latin-based words with no contractions, the marks of formal diction.

review.q: Which sentence uses connotation to take a side against the people described?
choices: The crowd moved toward the stage.
The mob swarmed toward the stage.
The audience walked toward the stage.
review.why: Mob and swarmed are loaded with danger, while the other sentences use neutral words.

review.q: A student writes 'hey can u move my exam' to a principal. What has gone wrong?
choices: The register does not fit the audience
review.why: The message is clear but pitched in a casual register that the situation does not call for.

review.q: A long sentence followed by a very short one usually creates what effect?
choices: A sharp impact on the short sentence
review.why: Contrast in length makes the short sentence land hard, like a slammed door.

review.q: 'Never have I seen such a mess' is an example of which technique?
review.why: The negative word leads and the verb comes before the subject, reversing normal order for emphasis.

choices: She passed the exam, after months of studying and two failed practice tests.
After months of studying and two failed practice tests, she passed the exam.
review.why: The main clause 'she passed the exam' is delayed until the end, which is what makes a sentence periodic.

review.q: In 'He checked the lock twice. Nothing. Just the wind.' what are 'Nothing' and 'Just the wind'?
review.why: They are short, set up by a complete sentence, and each carries one beat, the marks of a fragment used on purpose.

review.q: Which sentence puts the news in the position of greatest emphasis?
choices: The plant will close, the report recommended, after eleven months of study.
After eleven months of study, the report, which ran to two hundred pages, was released.
The report recommended closing the plant on a Tuesday in March.
The two-hundred-page report recommended closing the plant.
review.why: End focus gives the final words the most weight, and this version ends on 'closing the plant.'
